paragraphs.source_en: Turning left from the side street, there stood in the distance something like an extraordinarily tall, thick bamboo pole, with a faint wisp of smoke rising from its tip. This, namely, was the public bathhouse. I slipped quietly in through the back entrance; some may call that cowardice, or a sign of lingering attachment. In truth, such talk is nothing more than the grumbling of those who, out of a certain envy, insist one must always pay calls through the front door. From ancient times, clever people have always made surprise attacks by the back door; so it is written on page five, chapter one, volume two of The Method of Forming a Gentleman. On the next page of that same book there is even the maxim, “The back door is the testament of the gentleman, the gate by which he gains virtue for himself.” I am a cat of the twentieth century, and I have received at least this much education. It would therefore be best not to despise me too lightly. To return to the matter at hand: when I had slipped inside and looked about, split pine logs, sawed to about eight inches, were piled up like a mountain. Beside them, coal too was heaped high like a mound. Someone may ask why I say the pinewood is “like a mountain” and the coal “like a mound.” There is really no special meaning; I merely wished to use two different expressions. Humans eat rice, eat fowl, eat fish, even eat beasts, and after exhausting every manner of foul food, have at last sunk so low as to eat coal; it is pitiable indeed. Pressing on, I saw that an entrance about six feet wide stood thrown open. When I peered inside, it was hollow and deserted, with not the least sound. Yet from the room opposite there seemed to come human voices, and I immediately concluded that the so-called bathhouse must be somewhere around where those voices were issuing. I passed through the valley formed between the pinewood and the coal, turned left, and went forward; on the right was a glass window, and on this side of it a great many round little tubs were stacked in a triangle, that is, in the shape of a pyramid. For round things to be stacked into a triangle must surely be against their wishes, and in secret I sympathized with the feelings of the little tubs, my good fellows. To the south of the little tubs there remained four or five feet of board, appearing just as if it had been set there to welcome me. The board stood about one meter above the ground, making it perfectly made to order for me to leap up onto. “Excellent,” I said. With a light spring upward, the so-called bathhouse appeared at once before the tip of my nose. If one asks what in all the world is most amusing, surely nothing is so delightful as eating what one has never eaten and seeing what one has never seen. It is all very well if you, like my master, spend thirty or forty minutes in this bathing realm three times a week, but if, like me, you have never seen such a thing as a bath, then by all means go and look at one. You may miss being at your parents’ deathbed, but this sight you absolutely must see. Wide though the world may be, such a spectacle is exceedingly rare.

ja.t: ちピラミッドのごとく

units.source_zh: 我从松柴和煤堆的夹道儿当中穿过去，向左拐，再往前走，右侧有个玻璃窗子，在窗子这边，一大堆圆形小桶，摞成三角形，也就是说，是按金字塔形摞在那里。

units.source_en: For round things to be stacked into a triangle must surely be against their wishes, and in secret I sympathized with the feelings of the little tubs, my good fellows.
units.source_zh: 本来是圆形的东西，却被摞成三角形，这当然不是出于甘心情愿的，所以我对小桶诸君的心意还是可以谅解的。

units.source_en: To the south of the little tubs there remained four or five feet of board, appearing just as if it had been set there to welcome me.
units.source_zh: 在小桶的南边留有一段五六尺长的隔板，好像是为迎接我而专设的。

units.source_en: The board stood about one meter above the ground, making it perfectly made to order for me to leap up onto.
units.source_zh: 这隔板离地面有一米高，对我跳上去是再合适也不过的了。

units.source_en: “Excellent,” I said.
units.source_zh: 我说了声：“这太好啦。”

units.source_en: With a light spring upward, the so-called bathhouse appeared at once before the tip of my nose.
units.source_zh: 纵身往上一跳，所谓浴室就立即出现在我的鼻子尖前。

units.source_en: If one asks what in all the world is most amusing, surely nothing is so delightful as eating what one has never eaten and seeing what one has never seen.
units.source_zh: 如果说天下什么最有趣，那当然是能吃到从未吃过的东西，能看到从未看到的景物，这最能使人愉快了。

units.source_en: It is all very well if you, like my master, spend thirty or forty minutes in this bathing realm three times a week, but if, like me, you have never seen such a thing as a bath, then by all means go and look at one.
units.source_zh: 诸位当中如果也能像我家主人那样，每周三次在这种沐浴的世界里度过三四十分钟当然是再好不过了，假如您像我一样从未看见过洗澡这类事儿，那么请你一定去看看。

units.source_en: You may miss being at your parents’ deathbed, but this sight you absolutely must see.

paragraphs.source_zh: 从胡同往左拐，就有一根极高的粗大竹竿似的东西屹立在那里，上边还冒着淡淡的烟。这就是公共澡堂。我从后门偷偷地溜了进去，也许有人会说这是卑怯的表现，或恋恋不舍的表现。其实，这只不过是那些一定非从前门去拜访不可的人，出于某种嫉妒心理，说出来的牢骚话罢了。自古以来，聪明人总是从后门搞突然袭击的，这在《绅士养成法》的第二卷第一章第五页上就是这样写的。在这本书的下一页中还写有：“绅士的遗书中写有后门乃自身具备德性之门也”的话头。在下是二十世纪的猫儿，这样的教育我还是受过的。所以还是请勿小看我为妙。书归正传，当我溜进去一看，里面那些劈开的松木、锯成八寸来长的木柴堆积如山。在其旁，煤也堆成高高的土堆模样。也许有人要问，为什么说松柴就说它“如山”而把煤说成“土堆”呢？其实并无别的意思，我只不过想使用两种不同的说法而已。人吃米饭，又吃鸡吃鱼，还吃什么家畜，把种种糟糕的东西都吃全了，最后竟堕落到吃起煤来，真是可怜！我往前闯，一看，有个六尺宽的门敞开着。我往里一瞧，里边空空荡荡，一点响声也没有。而对面屋里好像有人声，我立即断定，所谓的澡堂肯定就在发出声音的那一带。我从松柴和煤堆的夹道儿当中穿过去，向左拐，再往前走，右侧有个玻璃窗子，在窗子这边，一大堆圆形小桶，摞成三角形，也就是说，是按金字塔形摞在那里。本来是圆形的东西，却被摞成三角形，这当然不是出于甘心情愿的，所以我对小桶诸君的心意还是可以谅解的。在小桶的南边留有一段五六尺长的隔板，好像是为迎接我而专设的。这隔板离地面有一米高，对我跳上去是再合适也不过的了。我说了声：“这太好啦。”纵身往上一跳，所谓浴室就立即出现在我的鼻子尖前。如果说天下什么最有趣，那当然是能吃到从未吃过的东西，能看到从未看到的景物，这最能使人愉快了。诸位当中如果也能像我家主人那样，每周三次在这种沐浴的世界里度过三四十分钟当然是再好不过了，假如您像我一样从未看见过洗澡这类事儿，那么请你一定去看看。您可以不给爹娘送终，但这个情景非看不可。天下虽大，却难得有这一奇观。
